notes: Bounces back up to Exodus-scale cast size (11 majors) after Leviticus's near-total lack of characters, as expected — Numbers is narrative-heavy again. Eleazar promoted from submanager (Exodus/Leviticus) to full manager here — succeeding Aaron as high priest (Numbers 20:25-28) is a book-specific pivotal event, same per-book-not-inherited rule as Nadab/Abihu in Leviticus. Zelophehad's five daughters are indexed as one major (Mahlah) plus four submanagers rather than five separate majors, since the text never differentiates their individual actions — they act and speak as one petitioning unit throughout (Numbers 27, 36).

characters.name: Moses

verses.note: 'Now the man Moses was very meek, above all the men which were upon the face of the earth'
Intercedes for Israel after the spies' report, averting destruction
Strikes the rock at Meribah in anger instead of speaking to it as commanded — barred from entering the promised land as a result
Commissions Joshua as his successor by the laying on of hands

funFacts: The consequence of striking the rock (Numbers 20:12) is arguably the single most personally costly moment in his entire story — barred from the one goal that has driven the whole journey since Exodus 3.

characters.name: Aaron

verses.note: Joins Miriam in opposing Moses over his Cushite wife; only Miriam is struck with leprosy
Runs into the plague with a censer to make atonement, stopping it — 'he stood between the dead and the living'
His rod alone, of the twelve tribal rods, buds, blossoms, and yields almonds overnight — confirms the Levitical priesthood
Dies on Mount Hor; his priestly garments transferred to Eleazar before his death

funFacts: This is a different rod-sign from the one in Exodus 7:9-12 (rod-to-serpent before Pharaoh) — the budding almond rod is specifically a Numbers event, confirming his priestly line rather than demonstrating power to Pharaoh.

characters.name: Miriam

verses.note: Speaks against Moses over his Cushite wife, is struck with leprosy, shut outside the camp seven days
Dies at Kadesh and is buried there

funFacts: Called 'the prophetess' back in Exodus 15:20 — the text never revokes that title even after Numbers 12, though it is notably her, not Aaron, who bears the punishment for the same complaint.

characters.name: Caleb

verses.note: One of the twelve spies, representing Judah; alone with Joshua, urges the people to trust God and go up
Promised entry into the land 'because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully'

funFacts: First appearance in scripture is here, in Numbers — he has no prior book presence the way Joshua does from Exodus.

characters.name: Joshua

verses.note: One of the twelve spies, representing Ephraim — named 'Oshea' until Moses renames him Joshua in this passage
With Caleb, tears his clothes and urges the people not to rebel against the LORD
Formally commissioned as Moses' successor

funFacts: Numbers 13:16 is where the name change from Oshea to Joshua is actually recorded — he was already called Joshua back in Exodus 17, so this verse is explaining, not introducing, the name.

characters.name: Korah

genealogy.father: izhar — Numbers 16:1, a Levite, not individually indexed

verses.note: Leads a Levite challenge to Aaron's exclusive priesthood, joined by Dathan, Abiram, and 250 princes
'The earth opened her mouth, and swallowed them up... and all that appertained to Korah'

funFacts: The 250 princes who joined him offering incense are not individually named — only Korah, Dathan, and Abiram are (see genealogyLists for the note on 'On the son of Peleth', who is named once at the start of the episode and then never mentioned again).

characters.name: Balaam

verses.note: Hired by Balak to curse Israel; his donkey (KJV: 'the ass') sees the angel of the LORD and speaks to him three times before his own eyes are opened
Blesses Israel four times instead of cursing them, against Balak's repeated demands
Killed later, during Israel's war against Midian

funFacts: Tier name uses 'donkey' rather than the KJV's own word 'ass' for UI clarity on a mobile screen — flagged here since the translation itself is being followed exactly everywhere else in this project; this is a display-label choice, not a text change.

verses.note: King of Moab; hires Balaam out of fear of Israel's numbers
Repeatedly builds altars and offers sacrifices, trying to get Balaam to curse Israel from a different vantage point

characters.name: Phinehas

verses.note: Drives a javelin through an Israelite man and a Midianite woman, stopping a plague sent for Israel's apostasy at Baal-peor
Rewarded with 'my covenant of peace... an everlasting priesthood' for his zeal

funFacts: Aaron's grandson, Eleazar's son — the priesthood promise here is what makes his line, not just Aaron's in general, specifically significant going forward.

characters.name: Eleazar

verses.note: Aaron's priestly garments are stripped from Aaron and put on him atop Mount Hor, just before Aaron dies
Assists Moses in taking the second census
Stands with Moses at Joshua's commissioning

funFacts: Promoted from submanager (in Exodus and Leviticus, where he's only named among Aaron's sons) to full manager here — succeeding his father as high priest is a book-specific pivotal event.

characters.name: Mahlah

verses.note: With her four sisters, petitions Moses for their father's inheritance since he died with no sons — the LORD rules in their favor, setting a lasting precedent
The ruling is refined — the sisters must marry within their own tribe so the inheritance doesn't pass out of it

funFacts: Named first of the five sisters every time they appear as a group (Numbers 27:1, 36:11) — the reason she's the one indexed as the major manager here, with her sisters as submanagers, rather than five separate tiers for five people who otherwise act as one unit throughout.

characters.name: Noah (Zelophehad's daughter)
characters.perkNote: Accuracy flag: a completely different person from Noah of the Flood (Genesis 6-9) — same KJV spelling, unrelated, different gender, thousands of years apart.

verses.note: Named second of the five sisters
Named third of the five sisters

characters.name: Milcah (Zelophehad's daughter)
characters.perkNote: Accuracy flag: a different person from Milcah, Nahor's wife back in Genesis 11:29 — same KJV spelling, unrelated.

verses.note: Named fourth of the five sisters
Named fifth of the five sisters

genealogy.father: eliab — Numbers 16:1, a Reubenite, not individually indexed

verses.note: Joins Korah's challenge; his household swallowed with Korah's

genealogy.father: eliab — Numbers 16:1, a Reubenite, not individually indexed

verses.note: Joins Korah's challenge alongside his brother Dathan
Prophesies in the camp without having gone to the tabernacle; Joshua wants them stopped, but Moses answers 'would God that all the LORD's people were prophets'
Prophesies alongside Eldad

characters.name: Hobab

verses.note: Invited by Moses to journey with Israel as a guide, 'instead of eyes' to them in the wilderness

funFacts: Accuracy flag, genuinely disputed: the Hebrew of Numbers 10:29 can be read as either Hobab himself being Moses' father-in-law, or Hobab being Raguel/Reuel's son and therefore Moses' brother-in-law (since Reuel/Jethro is established elsewhere as the father-in-law, see Exodus 2:18, 3:1). Not resolved here — flagged as an open textual question rather than silently picking one reading.

genealogy.father: salu — Numbers 25:14, a prince of Simeon, not individually indexed

verses.note: An Israelite prince, killed by Phinehas together with Cozbi at Baal-peor

genealogy.father: zur — Numbers 25:15, a Midianite chief, not individually indexed

verses.note: A Midianite woman, killed by Phinehas together with Zimri at Baal-peor

genealogyLists.note: Deferred names with no individual narrative action, or too thin to index individually.

onSonOfPeleth.note: Named once as one of Korah's initial group, then never mentioned again in the episode's outcome — a genuine textual curiosity, not something this project invents an explanation for.

amoriteKings.note: Named battle opponents with no independent action beyond being defeated; not given full entries.

twelveSpies.note: All twelve are named, one per tribe — only Caleb and Joshua are indexed individually here, since the other ten act as an undifferentiated group ('the men that brought up the evil report') and are struck down together (Numbers 14:36-37).
